newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan devaluation sets off bull run in Karachi.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan devaluation sets off bull run in Karachi.

text.p: Pakistan stocks soared for the second straight day on Wednesday after the government devalued the rupee 7.86 percent against the dollar and imposed tough new economic stabilisation measures.
But dealers said the next two months could prove crucial for the economy and for the Karachi Stock Exchange.

"Export-linked industry will get a boost and the trade deficit will go down because of the rupee devaluation," dealer Ather Raouf of Carr Mashriq said. "The market reacted positively as it had expected a worse scenario."
The government plans to narrow the budget gap by 40 billion rupees ($995 million) in 1996/97 (July-June) through spending cuts, extra taxes and a 10 percent rise in fuel prices.

The State (central) Bank of Pakistan raised its key repurchase discount rate to 20 percent a year from 17 percent. The package is intended to persuade the International Monetary Fund, which is sending a team to Islamabad on Thursday, to release tranches of a stalled $600 million standby loan.
"We know these steps will not solve Pakistan's economic problems in the near future, but at least they are in the right direction," Raouf said.
The Karachi 100-share index rose 38.94 points, or 2.79 percent, to a provisional 1,432.57 on Wednesday. On Tuesday it posted a gain of 29.01 points or 2.12 percent.

"The Pakistani market is sentiment-driven. It welcomed these steps because it appears that finally something is being done to stop the rot," said Nadeem Naqvi, head of research at International Asset Management Co.
"If this euphoria continues, the market could easily test 1,500 points in next few days."
Naqvi said cuts in government spending had little precedent in Pakistan and would have a genuine positive impact if they were followed by long-term structural reforms.

But he said the immediate result of the devaluation and higher interest rates could be a mini-recession. "Corporate earnings will go down and profit margins will be squeezed. The market has not yet looked at this aspect," he said.
He said foreign investors would stay in a wait-and-see mood for the next two months.
"Whether Pakistan is able to increase its exports and the government manages to contain its bank borrowing will decide the flow of investment in Pakistan," Naqvi said.

Naqvi said foreign investors might return to the market early next year if Pakistan won an IMF seal of approval and Moody's Investors' Services Inc held back from its threatened downgrade of Pakistani credit ratings.
Dealer Hina Akhlaq of KASB & Co said the latest gains could not be sustained as they were fuelled by speculators, who pushed up prices in thin trading, not by foreign buying.
She said the devaluation could help exports and local industries competing with imported goods. "The decision is certainly favourable for the export-oriented textile sector."

Taurus Securities' chief dealer, Manochar Jamal, said the telecom utility PTCL, which accounts for almost 40 percent of market capitalisation, stood to profit from the devaluation because of windfall gains on its foreign earnings.

He said the fuel and energy sector would also benefit from the devaluation and the increase in oil product prices. Local synthetics makers would gain an advantage over more expensive imported polyester staple fibre.
"But the cement sector will be hit by the government's decision to cut development expenses and its production cost will increase due to the rise in furnace oil prices," he said.
